talks.title: #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC API Security Through External Attack Surface Management
talks.teaser: Examines #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC API Security Through External Attack Surface Management and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Philip Wiley presents at HITB Singapore on API security through external attack surface management, drawing from his role as hacker-in-residence at Psycognito.

Key Topics: Continuous attack surface monitoring versus annual penetration tests; discovering vulnerabilities between assessment cycles; threat actor perspective on external-facing assets; and retest validation workflows.

Technical Details: Wiley describes finding high-severity API vulnerabilities during continuous monitoring that would have persisted until the next annual pen test. He emphasizes detecting assets the same way threat actors discover them.

Takeaways: Annual penetration tests leave year-long gaps in attack surface visibility. Organizations should implement continuous external attack surface management with threat actor perspective.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Fuzzing The MCU Of Connected Vehicles For Security And Safety
talks.teaser: Outlines #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Fuzzing The MCU Of Connected Vehicles For Security And Safety and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Automotive Domain Context

Huawei inspector Ho Chen (Flag Sky) explains modern vehicle domain architectures where HMI domains expose Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and cellular links while powertrain/chassis DCUs control safety-critical ESP/ABS functions—creating paths from infotainment compromise into vehicle control. Safety (unintentional failure) and security (malicious exploitation) both matter for MCU software.

MCU-Fuzz Tool Motivation

Traditional MCU testing relies on manual review, unit tests, and static analysis with coverage metrics, but vehicle-control systems need stronger assurance. Chen proposes MCU-Fuzz to apply coverage-guided fuzzing to domain-controller MCU firmware, complementing rather than replacing existing methods.

Hardware-Assisted Design

Automotive MCUs like NXP S32G offer limited RAM, Autosar RTOS without MMU, and GCC constraints that block common AFL injection. MCU-Fuzz uses embedded trace macrocell (ETM) hardware debug trace for coverage feedback instead of software instrumentation, enabling intelligent fuzzing where conventional host fuzzers cannot run directly on-target.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Faking At Level 1: How Digital Twins Save Your PLCs
talks.teaser: Provides #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Faking At Level 1: How Digital Twins Save Your PLCs and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
OT Foundations and Risk

Thomas, an embedded IoT security researcher, explains operational technology spanning PLCs, RTUs, HMIs, and SCADA across Purdue model levels. Unlike IT pen tests, OT assessments risk physical process disruption, lengthy recovery, and rare maintenance windows where even port scans can reboot hundreds of PLCs.

IT Versus OT Constraints

OT networks run low-bandwidth, hard real-time control traffic. A brief failure can halt factories for weeks, especially in chemical plants. Automated scanners are unsafe; testers must coordinate closely with plant operators and log all network activity.

Firmware Digital Twins

The talk focuses on firmware digital twins: emulated copies of device operating systems that run without physical hardware. This enables security research on level-one controllers when buying or fuzzing real PLCs is impractical, though emulation introduces fidelity tradeoffs vendors are still addressing.

Faking Level 1 for Safer Testing

By simulating PLCs and related level-one devices, teams can explore vulnerabilities and defensive controls without touching live production equipment. Thomas positions digital twins as a bridge between OT security assessment needs and the safety requirements of industrial environments.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Building An Army Of Bots By Hijacking a Twitter Handle
talks.teaser: Details #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Building An Army Of Bots By Hijacking a Twitter Handle and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
From mobile privacy to secrets

Rahul and Vishal explain how their BeVisual mobile privacy project evolved into broader mobile-app security research. They responsibly disclosed findings to affected vendors after discovering widespread hard-coded secrets in Android and iOS applications indexed at scale.

Scale of exposed credentials

Scanning hundreds of thousands of apps, they found hard-coded AWS API keys, Firebase URLs with default write access, Zendesk keys exposing support tickets, and more. They built over 200 YARA-style signatures to hunt these patterns automatically across decompiled packages.

BeVisual analysis pipeline

Their platform decompiles apps with tools like JADX, performs static analysis, and uses grep-style pattern matching to surface leaked keys. The talk connects mobile supply-chain risk—where backend credentials ship inside consumer apps—to downstream abuse such as bot armies and infrastructure takeover when handles or APIs are compromised.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN #LAB Advanced Code Obfuscation With MBA Expressions
talks.teaser: Analyzes #HITB2022SIN #LAB Advanced Code Obfuscation With MBA Expressions and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk places code obfuscation among the technical protections used against man-at-the-end attacks, where an analyst controls both the binary and its environment. It then introduces mixed Boolean-arithmetic (MBA) expressions, which combine arithmetic and bitwise operators. The speaker contrasts their use in obfuscation with cryptography: there, complex syntax reflects complex behaviour, whereas obfuscation hides a simple behaviour behind a complicated form.

Several transformations are demonstrated with live coding and checked with the Z3 SMT solver. MBA rewriting swaps an operator for an equivalent expression, and composition lets such rules be applied repeatedly. Insertion of identities wraps an expression in a pair of inverse affine functions, growing it while preserving its meaning. Opaque constants hide a target value behind permutation polynomials and a non-trivial expression that always evaluates to zero. Further demos show opaque predicates that add fake branches to control flow, and a small custom virtual machine whose handlers are obfuscated with MBA rewriting, making its opcode semantics harder to map.

The main takeaway is that these transforms complicate both data flow and control flow, and that they become stronger when combined with other techniques. The speaker notes that methods for generating inverse permutation polynomials remain an open research area. Demo code and references are shared in a public repository, giving reverse engineers and researchers a starting point for studying this kind of protection.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Exploiting Race Condition Vulnerabilities In Web Applications
talks.teaser: Presents #HITB2022SIN #COMMSEC Exploiting Race Condition Vulnerabilities In Web Applications and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with what a race condition is: several processes access shared data, and timing decides the result. Such bugs are hard to test because reproducing them depends on milliseconds, so penetration tests often overlook them. Examples include bypassing rate limits, overspending a bank balance, casting repeated votes, and reusing single-use tokens. Two large bug bounty cases were shown: a rate limit on a six-digit reset code at AWS Cognito was bypassed with over a thousand attempts, and password reset and login flaws at Instagram and Microsoft led to account takeover.

A short PHP withdrawal function shows a gap between the balance check and the balance update. The speaker suggests locking, a conditional update that compares the old value so changes can be detected, and a single atomic statement. A vulnerable demo application was then built on PHP and MariaDB, and a WAF, runtime protection, static analysis and DAST all missed its race condition. The speaker reviewed tools such as Turbo Intruder and proposed a distributed tool that sends requests from several servers near the target; with two servers, the average gap between requests reaching the target was about 1.92 milliseconds. A live demo bypassed a one-vote-per-user limit.

The conclusion is that finding these flaws requires business logic knowledge and manual testing, because the automated tools tested did not catch them. The speaker urged more awareness of this under-researched area, and the tool is published on GitHub.
